analysis.one_liner: Bars states from banning any FDA-approved contraceptive drug or device.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar state bans on FDA-approved contraception was introduced in May 2023, referred to committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit states from banning any contraceptive drug or device that the FDA has approved or authorized for contraception. It would preserve state control over medical practice and would not override federal religious-freedom law or state laws letting entities refuse to provide contraception on religious or moral grounds. The bill never moved after referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and other people who use contraception gain a federal guarantee that no state can ban an FDA-approved contraceptive drug or device, protecting access to birth control pills, IUDs, implants, and emergency contraception from state-level political decisions. Contraceptive manufacturers also gain a protected national market for their products.

how_it_helps.text: It bars states from banning the prescription, provision, or use of any contraceptive drug or device that the FDA has approved, licensed, cleared, or otherwise authorized.
It guarantees that a state-level political decision cannot remove an FDA-approved contraceptive from the market within that state.

analysis.who_pays: State governments that might want to restrict contraception lose that power, and religious or morally objecting providers would remain shielded by explicit carve-outs. Taxpayers bear no direct cost, as the bill creates no new program.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly does not override the Religious Freedom Restoration Act or state laws letting providers, employers, or other entities refuse to provide contraception on religious or moral grounds, so even where a ban is barred, access could still be blocked by individual refusals.

It is limited to FDA-approved contraceptive drugs, biologics, and devices; it does not by itself expand access, affordability, or insurance coverage, and it leaves states free to regulate the practice of medicine and pharmacy.
By overriding state policy choices on a contested health issue, the bill removes state-level decision-making, which opponents of federal preemption would object to on federalism grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — guaranteeing that no state can ban FDA-approved contraception — is real given post-Dobbs uncertainty, and the cost is limited because the bill preserves state authority over medical practice and conscience exemptions, so states retain substantial regulatory room. The main weakness is that by leaving exemptions in place, it would not guarantee actual access everywhere it bans bans. It never received any committee action, so no version was ever tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2023, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and no further action of any kind was recorded for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The bill's status is 'Died in a previous Congress,' confirming no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
All six cosponsors were Republicans, showing at least some cross-ideological interest within the majority party, but the bill never reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No group gained directly from the bill's death, but states that might want to restrict contraception retained full freedom of action, and no restrictions were lifted.

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Bice
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, to bar state bans on FDA-approved contraception.

for.name: Reps. Young Kim, Lloyd Smucker, Don Bacon, Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and Garret Graves
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee and took no further action on it for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only six sponsors and cosponsors were all Republicans, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote to reveal broader party or bipartisan positions.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical and medical device makers of contraceptive products
industries.note: By barring state bans on FDA-approved contraceptives, the bill protects the nationwide market for their products, a modest gain; it imposes no new costs. Its importance to the industry is limited since most contraceptive products are not under threat of state bans.

industries.industry: State governments seeking to restrict reproductive health products
industries.note: States lose the power to ban FDA-approved contraceptive products within their borders, which is precisely the constraint on state power the bill is designed to create.
